title: EXPLODE your Chest Gains (3 KILLER Pec Exercises)
summary: When bench or dip progress stalls or the joints complain, NH says to keep the main press but spread chest volume over other movements. He teaches three: the Spoto press (pause just above the chest), a chest fly where the stretch comes from opening the chest rather than straightening the arms, and a guillotine ring push-up with open elbows aimed at the upper chest.
claims: Chest training should be simple: pick a press you enjoy, like bench or dips, stick with it and progress
Pressing progress eventually stalls unless you perma-bulk; then diversify movements to challenge the chest in other planes and break the bench plateau
Always doing the same press eventually brings shoulder or elbow pain; give your favourite lift a rest and get volume from other movements without dropping the main press
The Spoto press is a bench press paused just shy of the chest; it keeps the chest under tension in the stretched position, unlike a regular pause bench where the bar rests on the chest
Pause benching keeps you stable and tight, with level shoulders and no rebound off the chest
Touch-and-go let him bench more, but every rep degraded his form: his arch died, his chest dropped and his shoulders took over
On the Spoto press you tend to fail suddenly (rep 8 easy, rep 9 impossible) because the chest is the limiting factor, so always use a spotter
Hold the Spoto pause 1-2 seconds without clearing the last portion of the range and then bouncing up; done right, the chest, not the triceps, limits the set
Touching the chest is a powerlifting requirement, not a hypertrophy one; the closer the bar is to the chest the more the chest works, so the Spoto press keeps you in that range longer
Never go below 6 reps on the Spoto press; 6-10, 8-10 or 8-12 all work
Straight-arm chest flies with minimal elbow bend only make the lift mechanically harder: you lift less weight for less stimulus, and the position is bad for the shoulder
For flies, keep a fixed elbow bend with the elbows tight and create the stretch by puffing the chest up and expanding the rib cage; the chest opens, not the arms
Stop the fly descent when the weights are roughly in line with the chest; going deeper adds nothing, just as the bench press stops at the chest
Flies are not a baby-weight exercise; use loads that push you to failure and beyond
The top squeeze is widely overrated for hypertrophy; the controlled descent and stretch are what matter
A fly should feel comfortable; any shoulder discomfort means your form needs fixing
The whole chest works as a unit; the bench press and dips develop the upper chest and no special movement is mandatory, though one that lets you feel it more is worth doing
The guillotine press is risky because touching high on the clavicle forces a lot of internal shoulder rotation and less weight
Ring push-ups solve the tucked-versus-open-elbow dilemma because the wrists are free; with a fixed bar the shoulder absorbs all the rotation
Guillotine ring push-up: let the elbows flare, touch the rings to the upper chest, keep the forearms perpendicular to the floor, and let opening the chest create the stretch
Do guillotine ring push-ups for 10-12, 10-15 or as many reps as possible, weighted with a backpack if needed, keeping every rep identical; doing them pre-fatigued suits advanced lifters
Deficit ring push-ups are unnecessary: once the hand touches the body you have most of the stretch, and going further mostly stretches tendons
exercises: pause 1-2 s just above the chest, stay tight, no bounce; spotter needed
stretched-position tension, chest is limiting factor, shoulder-friendly
fixed elbow bend, elbows tight, puff chest, stop in line with chest
full chest stretch with heavier loads and safe shoulders
elbows flare, rings touch upper chest, forearms vertical
upper-chest stretch without fixed-bar shoulder stress
stable and tight but chest relaxes on the pause
